steps.prompt: List all the divisors of $72$. How many are there? Is there a faster way than listing?
steps.placeholder: I count… a faster way might be…

cards.title: Add one, then multiply
cards.body: If $n = p^a \cdot q^b \cdot r^c$, a divisor picks a power of $p$ from $0$ to $a$ ($a + 1$ choices), a power of $q$ from $0$ to $b$, and so on. So $n$ has $(a + 1)(b + 1)(c + 1)$ positive divisors.

cards.title: Worked example: divisors of 72
cards.problem: How many positive divisors does $72$ have?

try.prompt: How many positive divisors does $72$ have?

cards.title: Special kinds of divisors
cards.body: Even divisors must use at least one $2$: for $2^3 \cdot 3^2$ that is $3 \times 3 = 9$. Odd divisors use no $2$: $1 \times 3 = 3$. Square divisors use even powers only. And only perfect squares have an odd number of divisors, because divisors pair up as $d$ and $\frac{n}{d}$.

cards.title: Worked example: the sum of the divisors
cards.problem: What is the sum of the positive divisors of $72$?

steps.text: Every divisor is (a power of $2$) $\times$ (a power of $3$), so the sum is $(1 + 2 + 4 + 8)(1 + 3 + 9)$.

try.prompt: What is the sum of the divisors of $72$?

cards.title: The common trap: forgetting the +1
cards.body: The power $0$ counts too (it gives the divisor $1$ for that prime), so add one to each exponent before you multiply: $2^3 \cdot 3^2$ has $4 \times 3 = 12$ divisors, not $3 \times 2 = 6$. And always factor completely first: $72 = 8 \times 9$ is not yet in primes.

prompts: Why does a perfect square have an odd number of divisors? Explain it in your own words.
